The cores enclose the lift shafts, stairs and provide overall lateral stability to the blocks. The walls are connected by lintel beams over the door openings. Block A1 also features a shear wall separating two apartments (Figure 21) to satisfy h/300 sway limit under wind loading, where h is a storey height. The floor slabs act as horizontal diaphragms, transferring the lateral loads imposed on the cladding back to the stability cores, the resulting overturning (vertical push-pull) and sliding (lateral) reaction forces are resisted by the core cap foundations. It is assumed that the slabs are connected to the reinforced concrete walls via a proprietary system e.g. Kwikastrip. This provides flexibility in terms of the method of construction of the core walls. Each of the blocks has one central core, independent of the other blocks. The movement joint at podium level avoids indirectly sharing lateral loads between blocks based on the relative stiffness of the cores for any given wind direction. At this stage the lateral stability of each block has been assessed independently of other blocks where not broken by the movement joint. This ensures each block has sufficient lateral stability without reliance on another block. Typical core layouts plans are shown in Figure 21.

Barratt London   Crown Wharf (Canning Town Riverside) Block A  | C05 | 4 November 2025 | Ove Arup & Partners Scotland Limited   Structural Basis of Design   Page 14  Figure 20 Cross-Section View Through Blocks A2 and A3 Showing the Podium Structure Figure 21 Plan View of the Podium Level Slab with the Vertical Movement Joint Highlighted  3.5   Podium  3.5.1   Overview The podium slab supports a landscaped accessible area between the blocks. The odium is constructed using a 450mm thick slab to accommodate the heavier landscaping loading. A vertical movement joints have been provided between each of the blocks at the podium slab to separate the blocks and control shrinkage stresses (Figure 21). Double vertical structure has been provided along the movement joint to support the slabs along the interface. The gap along the movement joint will be sealed by a propriety product to ensure weather tightness. The podium slab covers an underground car park, employment spaces, communal amenity space, car parking, cycle parking and refuse storage. The column positions for the central zone were coordinated with the architects to achieve the required layout and vehicle manoeuvring clearances.

Barratt London   Crown Wharf (Canning Town Riverside) Block A  | C05 | 4 November 2025 | Ove Arup & Partners Scotland Limited   Structural Basis of Design   Page 15  Figure 23 Pilecap Layout and Perimeter Retention  3.6   Foundations and Substructure  3.6.1   Piling and Basement Slab The foundation scheme utilises discrete pile groups and pile caps at the base of the columns and cores. Pile caps vary between 1600mm and 2400mm deep and have been optimised based on their associated column or core loads (Figure 23). Piles founded in the London Clay transfer the loads from the building deeper into the ground and reduce the settlement compared to a raft solution. All piles are to be 750 mm diameter for Block A1-A3 (or as per the Keller Piling design), while the piles supporting the concrete core of Block A4 are to be 900mm diameter (or as per the Keller Piling design). The groundwater level is taken as 5.600mOD. Due to the ground conditions, the basement slab is typically a 300mm thick reinforced concrete suspended slab, spanning between the pile caps. There is an area of slab running down the West side of the basement where the slab is 450mm thick to accommodate the high hydrostatic pressures. There are some steps and folds within the slab for changing levels and thicknesses. Lift pits are also provided within the core caps at the base of each lift shaft. The substructure has been designed for a varying hydrostatic pressure of 53 kPa at the West end of the basement dropping off to 0kPa in a linear fashion towards the Bidder Street end of the basement to the East. The West end of the basement has the bottom of the basement slab at 5.3m below the top of the podium slab, thus a hydrostatic pressure of 53kPa can be generated at this end. To the East end of the basement, the slab aligns closely with proposed external ground levels.  The characteristics of the London Clay layer give rise to a phenomenon referred to as ‘heave’ as the material swells after excavation. Due to the magnitude of the heave uplift force, it has been more economical for the substructure design to provide a proprietary heave board, such as Cordek Heaveguard rather than design the structure to resist the uplift forces. The substructure is designed for a relatively small differential heave based on the crushing capacity of the heave board above the self-weight of the basement slab. Barratt London   Crown Wharf (Canning Town Riverside) Block A  | C05 | 4 November 2025 | Ove Arup & Partners Scotland Limited   Structural Basis of Design   Page 16  Figure 24 Axonometric View of the Perimeter Retaining Walls  3.6.2   Basement and Retaining Structures Block A has a single-storey basement, retained by a 450mm thick in-situ reinforced concrete retaining wall along almost entire perimeter of the site, apart of the East part of the blocks, to align with future ground levels across the site (Figure 24). Space limitations on the boundary of the plot mean that along the North and West sides, the excavation may require temporary retention. The basement is to be tanked to achieve Grade 2 waterproofing to all residents lobbies, plant rooms, risers and store rooms. The basement is to be tanked to achieve Grade 1B waterproofing to car parking and bike store areas. The tanking strategies are to the specialist waterproofing contractors design (Premcrete). However, the strategy is use of Type A and Type B protection measures throughout. The proposed Type A protection is through a pre-applied membrane and the Type B protection gained through integral waterproof concrete.
